title: Anselm, Aquinas, and scholasticism
note: Scholastics used logic and disputation to understand faith. Anselm argued that God, that than which nothing greater can be thought, must exist in reality. Aquinas held that reason can prove God exists, giving the Five Ways, and that natural law is the rational creature's share in God's eternal law.

read.title: Proving God by reason
text: Anselm of Canterbury began from faith but wanted to understand what he believed. In the Proslogion he defined God as that than which nothing greater can be thought. Even the fool who denies God understands this phrase, so such a being exists at least in the mind. But a being that existed in reality as well would be greater. So if the greatest conceivable being existed only in the mind, a greater one could be thought, which is a contradiction. Therefore it exists in reality. The monk Gaunilo replied that the same reasoning would prove a perfect island; Anselm answered that his argument applies only to the greatest conceivable being.

Thomas Aquinas preferred to argue from the world. His Five Ways begin from things we observe: motion, causation, things that can come to be and pass away, degrees of goodness, and natural things acting for ends. Each reasons from such facts to a first source that depends on nothing else, which everyone calls God; the first three argue that an endless chain of dependent causes could explain nothing. Aquinas held that reason can know God exists, while doctrines such as the Trinity are known by revelation. Faith and reason, he insisted, cannot truly conflict, since both come from the same God.
